newsitem.title: GREECE: ATHLETICS-NEBIOLO SAYS WORLD CHAMPS TEST FOR ATHENS.
newsitem.headline: ATHLETICS-NEBIOLO SAYS WORLD CHAMPS TEST FOR ATHENS.

text.p: International Amateur Athletics Federation (IAAF) President Primo Nebiolo said on Thursday that Athens' bid for the 2004 Olympics would depend on how well it hosts the world athletics championship next year.
"If Greece is bidding for 2004 and it can't organise the world championship, then this bid must be withdrawn," Nebiolo told Reuters in an interview.

A year-long stubborn power game between the Greek sports ministry and the Greek Athletics Federation (SEGAS) on who has the upper hand in organising the event next August had angered the IAAF, which sent several warnings to both bodies.

"All people want to be number one and it is not easy to accept to be number two or three. I believe this internal problem is now solved. I have the guarantees of the government and SEGAS and I believe we will have a great edition of world championship," Nebiolo said.

"The world championship is the greatest sports event of 1997. We will have the best athletes and thousands of journalists. Greece is lucky to have this event, the biggest since it hosted the Olympics in 1896," he added.
SEGAS, which has signed a contract with the IAAF to run the championship, withdrew last month from its organising committee, complaining it was being marginalised by the sports ministry.

But both Sports Minister Andreas Fouras and SEGAS President Stratos Molivas were at the Athens airport on Wednesday to greet Nebiolo who arrived on a three-day visit for talks with Prime Minister Costas Simitis and other officials.

"They have finally understood that they must work together, at least until the end of the championship. It took much effort to make them realise that the event would be wrecked if this strife went on," a senior Greek sports official said.
Nebiolo said that Greece had the ability and the facilities to organise the world championship.
"Athens has a fantastic stadium and a great tradition in athletics," he said. "I believe that if Greeks are united they will have no problems."
Nebiolo, an Italian and one of the most influential figures in world sports, may be the decisive factor if the race for the 2004 Olympic Games comes down between Athens and Rome.

"I believe that both the Athens and Rome candidacies are very strong. If we will have a fight it must be a very fair fight. I want to be the first to shake the winner's hand and if Athens wins I'll be happy to shake hands with my Greek friends."
"Both cities deserve to organise the Olympic Games. Both will be very good organisers and I hope that they will be the two finalists. This will be fantastic, " he said.
Athens lost this year's Games to Atlanta mostly because of poor inftrastructure. It had threatened to boycott the centennial Olympic festivities in Atlanta and never bid for the Games again.

But it has since changed its mind and put together a much better bidding dossier for the 2004 Games. Sport officials say it is considered among the favourites along with Rome, Cape Town and Stockholm. Altogether 11 cities have made bids.
"The United States had the chance to organise the Olympics five times. Now we have to change," Nebiolo said.
